VEGANScreener + metabolomics

Q3: Associations between hPDI and the metabolome in vegans.

This script explores patterns in the metabolome profiles of vegans, particularly by linking them to the PDI score.

The script is divided into two parts, based on how the metabolome datasets were integrated (see the preprocessing scripts for details). The first part analyzes the sPCA dataset, which is used for multivariate analysis, PCA visualization, PERMANOVA, and the machine-learning models. The second part uses the concatenated dataset (LC-MS and NMR combined) for the univariate analysis.

The analysis is composed of the following main parts:

  1. Global visualization — the first three components, color-coded by hPDI.

  2. PERMANOVA — how much of the variation can be explained by various external variables: dist(Metabolome) ~ sex + bmi + age + veganDuration + country*hPDI

  3. Univariate analysis (feature-wise model) — linear modelling of each metabolite against various external variables: Metabolite ~ sex + bmi + age + veganDuration + Country*hPDI

  4. Random forest (RF) classification — the model is trained and validated by bootstrapping with 500 iterations, and used to distinguish between participants in the 1st and 3rd tertiles of hPDI. Two types of models are trained:

  1. a model on the original sPCA dataset
  2. a model on the sPCA dataset after regressing out the covariates.

1 Import

metadata_df <- read.table(
  file =  "../../data/preprocessed/metadata_preprocessed_v3.tsv",
  header = TRUE) 

lcms_df <- read.table(
  file= "../../data/preprocessed/metabolomics/lc_ms_preprocessed_INT_v3.tsv",
  check.names = FALSE)

nmr_df <- read.table(
  file = "../../data/preprocessed/metabolomics/nmr_preprocessed_INT_v3.tsv",
  check.names = FALSE) 

spca_integrated_df <-  read.table(
  file = "../../data/preprocessed/metabolomics/spca_integrated_vegans_INT_v3.tsv",
  check.names = FALSE) 

pdi_df <- read.table(
  file = "../../data/preprocessed/dietary/pdi/pdi_avg_residuals_scaled_v3.tsv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  header = TRUE) %>% 
  dplyr::select(study_id,pdi_avg,hpdi_avg,updi_avg) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(hpdi_avg = hpdi_avg + 30,
               updi_avg = updi_avg + 30)

metadata_df <- merge(metadata_df,pdi_df,by = "study_id",all.x = TRUE)
metadata_df <- metadata_df %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(hpdi_avg))
nmr_df <- nmr_df %>% dplyr::filter(rownames(.) %in% metadata_df$study_id)
lcms_df <- lcms_df %>% dplyr::filter(rownames(.) %in% metadata_df$study_id)
spca_integrated_df <- spca_integrated_df %>% dplyr::filter(rownames(.) %in% metadata_df$study_id)

Scaling — when metadata columns are used as covariates, they need to be scaled so that each has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

metadata_scaled_df <- metadata_df
metadata_scaled_df[,-c(1,3,5,6,8)] <- apply(metadata_df[,-c(1,3,5,6,8)],2,scale)
metadata_scaled_df <- metadata_scaled_df %>%
  mutate(sex=as.factor(sex),
         country=as.factor(country),
         group=as.factor(group),
         diet_supplements=as.factor(diet_supplements))

3 SPCA

The sPCA dataset was created by concatenating the LC-MS and NMR datasets and applying the mixOmics::spca() function. See the preprocessing script for details.

mixOmics::spca() performs sparse Principal Component Analysis (sPCA), which works like regular PCA but adds a sparsity constraint so that only a subset of variables contributes to each component. The degree of sparsity is controlled by a penalization term, which makes the components easier to interpret because irrelevant or noisy variables are given loadings of zero.

3.2 PERMANOVA

The test shows how much of the variation in the metabolome is explained by sex, age, BMI, vegan duration, country, and hPDI.

Variables were added sequentially (Type I sums of squares), so each p-value and R² reflects a partial effect after adjusting for the variables above it. The model first accounts for variation due to sex, age, vegan diet duration, BMI, and country of origin. It then accounts for the main effect of PDI, and finally tests whether the effect of PDI varies by country of origin (the interaction term).

PDI explains 1.873% of the variation after adjusting for sex, age, BMI, country, and diet duration. This result is statistically significant (p=0.001).

# Create Euclidean distance matrix
dist_mat <- vegdist(spca_integrated_df, 
                    method = "euclidean")

# Test whether vegan vs omnivore differ in metabolomics
adonis_result <- adonis2(
  dist_mat ~ sex + bmi + age + vegan_duration + country*hpdi_avg,
  data = metadata_scaled_df , 
  permutations = 999,
  by="terms")

print(adonis_result)

3.3 RF model

3.3.1 Original model

sub_metadata_df <- metadata_df %>%
dplyr::filter(
  tertile_label %in% c("1st_hPDItertile","3rd_hPDItertile"))

sub_spca_integrated_df <- spca_integrated_df[as.character(sub_metadata_df$study_id),]
model_name <- "hPDI_tertile_vegan" 

prepared_df <- model_preparation(sub_spca_integrated_df,
                                 sub_metadata_df,
                                 predicting_col = "tertile_label")

rf_model <- make_rf_model(data=prepared_df,
                            outcome="Group",
                            N = 500,
                           file = model_name,
                            reuse=TRUE)

roc_c <- roc_curve(model_object = rf_model, 
                   group = c("low hPDI","high hPDI"),CI = TRUE) 

roc_c <- ggtheme(roc_c) + 
  theme(legend.position="none",title = element_text(size=8))

roc_c

png 
  2

Accuracy

# Find the "best" threshold using Youden's J Index
# This maximizes (Sensitivity + Specificity - 1)
roc_obj <- rf_model$rocobj
best_threshold_data <- coords(roc_obj, "best", 
                              ret = "threshold", 
                              best.method = "youden")
optimal_threshold <- best_threshold_data$threshold
optimal_threshold

3.4 RF importance

3.4.1 Original model

PC5 and PC10 are the most important variables for the RF model.

load("../intermediate_files/models/hPDI_tertile_vegan/rf_model.RData")

var_imp <- as.data.frame(importance(rf_model$trained_model)) %>%
  rownames_to_column("PC") %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("PC","Importance")) 

var_imp <- var_imp %>% dplyr::mutate(PC=factor(PC,levels = PC[order(var_imp$Importance,decreasing = TRUE)])) 

ggplot(var_imp) + 
  geom_col(aes(x=PC,y=Importance))

3.4.2 Adjusted model

The most important variables are PC5 and PC1.

load("../intermediate_files/models/adjusted_hpdi_model_vegan/rf_model.RData")

var_imp <- as.data.frame(importance(rf_model$trained_model)) %>%
  rownames_to_column("PC") %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("PC","Importance")) 

var_imp <- var_imp %>% dplyr::mutate(PC=factor(PC,levels = PC[order(var_imp$Importance,decreasing = TRUE)])) 

ggplot(var_imp) + 
  geom_col(aes(x=PC,y=Importance))

4.2 Univariate analysis

We test the differences between diets and hPDI using a generalized linear model, while adjusting for covariates.

4.2.1 Continuous analysis

A GLM is used to identify which metabolites are significantly related to the hPDI score, adjusting for age, sex, country, and dietary group:

Metabolite ~ sex + bmi + age + eq_vegan_dur_total + Country*hPDI

results_list <- lapply(colnames(concat_integrated_df), 
                       function(x) fit_glm(x,concat_for_uni,
                                           tested_variable = "hpdi_avg"))
results_df <- do.call(rbind, results_list)

results_df$p_adjusted <- p.adjust(results_df$Pr...t..,method = "BH")

Significant results — 12 metabolites:

6 Metabolite-based hPDI

6.1 Continuous univariate test

To build a vegan index from the concatenated dataset, we use linear regression to obtain coefficients for the significant variables identified across the analysis:

final_significance
 [1] "PC.34.1."           "SM.d38.2."          "SM.d42.2."         
 [4] "SM.d34.1."          "SM.d32.1."          "Indoleacrylic.acid"
 [7] "LysoPC.17.0."       "Octenoylcarnitine"  "Ergothionenine"    
[10] "Acetylornithin"     "Glutamine"          "2-Hydroxybutyrate" 
sign <- final_significance
# define the variables
plot_list <- list()
rhos <- rep(NA,5)
ps <- rep(NA,5)

# split the datasets for cross-validation
concat_for_index <- concat_for_uni[sample(rownames(concat_for_uni)),]
set.seed(123)
cv_splits <- cv_folds(concat_for_index,folds = 5)

final_df_veganindex <- data.frame()

# cross validation loop
vars_selection <- list()
for (i in 1:length(cv_splits)){
  unisub_df <- concat_for_uni[cv_splits[[i]]$train,]
  results_list <- lapply(colnames(concat_integrated_df), 
                       function(x) fit_glm(x,unisub_df,
                                           tested_variable = "hpdi_avg"))
  results_df <- do.call(rbind, results_list)
  
  results_df$p_adjusted <- p.adjust(results_df$Pr...t..,method = "BH")

  vars <- results_df$metabolite[results_df$p_adjusted<0.05 & results_df$variable=="hpdi_avg"]
  vars_selection[[i]] <- vars
  
  # Wrap all variable names in backticks
  vars_safe <- paste0("`", vars, "`")
  
  fml <- as.formula(paste("hpdi_avg ~", paste(vars_safe, collapse = " + ")))
  
  # fit the model
  model <- lm(fml, unisub_df)
  
  # predict the result on validation dataset
  VG_index <- stats::predict(model,concat_for_uni[cv_splits[[i]]$val,])
  
  # store the predicted index
  sub_df <- concat_for_uni[cv_splits[[i]]$val,]
  sub_df$VGindex <- VG_index
  final_df_veganindex <- rbind(final_df_veganindex,sub_df)
  
  # calculate correlation 
  cor_test <- cor.test(sub_df$VGindex,
               sub_df$hpdi_avg,
               method = "spearman")
  cor_val <- cor_test$estimate
  if (cor_test$p.value >0.05) cor_val = 0

  # plot the result
  p <- ggplot(sub_df, 
              aes_string(x = "VGindex", y = "hpdi_avg"),
              color="blue") +
       geom_point() + 
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
    theme_minimal() + 
    ggtitle(paste("Rho =",round(cor_val,2)))

  plot_list[[i]] <- p
  rhos[i] <- round(cor_val,2)
  ps[i] <- cor_test$p.value
}

**This script explores patterns in the metabolome profiles of vegans, particularly by linking them to the PDI score.**


The script is divided into two parts, based on how the metabolome datasets were integrated (see the preprocessing scripts for details). The first part analyzes the **sPCA dataset**, which is used for multivariate analysis, PCA visualization, PERMANOVA, and the machine-learning models. The second part uses the **concatenated dataset** (LC-MS and NMR combined) for the univariate analysis. 

The analysis is composed of the following main parts:

1.  Global visualization — the first three components, color-coded by **hPDI**.

2.  PERMANOVA — how much of the variation can be explained by various external variables:
  dist(Metabolome) \~ sex + bmi + age + veganDuration + country***hPDI**

3.  Univariate analysis (feature-wise model) — linear modelling of each metabolite against various external variables:
  Metabolite \~  sex + bmi + age + veganDuration + Country***hPDI**
  
4.  Random forest (RF) classification — the model is trained and validated by bootstrapping with 500 iterations, and used to distinguish between participants in the **1st and 3rd tertiles of hPDI**. Two types of models are trained:
a) a model on the original sPCA dataset
b) a model on the sPCA dataset after regressing out the covariates.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
source("custom_functions_vegans.R")
```

# Import

```{r}
metadata_df <- read.table(
  file =  "../../data/preprocessed/metadata_preprocessed_v3.tsv",
  header = TRUE) 

lcms_df <- read.table(
  file= "../../data/preprocessed/metabolomics/lc_ms_preprocessed_INT_v3.tsv",
  check.names = FALSE)

nmr_df <- read.table(
  file = "../../data/preprocessed/metabolomics/nmr_preprocessed_INT_v3.tsv",
  check.names = FALSE) 

spca_integrated_df <-  read.table(
  file = "../../data/preprocessed/metabolomics/spca_integrated_vegans_INT_v3.tsv",
  check.names = FALSE) 

pdi_df <- read.table(
  file = "../../data/preprocessed/dietary/pdi/pdi_avg_residuals_scaled_v3.tsv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  header = TRUE) %>% 
  dplyr::select(study_id,pdi_avg,hpdi_avg,updi_avg) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(hpdi_avg = hpdi_avg + 30,
               updi_avg = updi_avg + 30)

metadata_df <- merge(metadata_df,pdi_df,by = "study_id",all.x = TRUE)
```

```{r}
metadata_df <- metadata_df %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(hpdi_avg))
nmr_df <- nmr_df %>% dplyr::filter(rownames(.) %in% metadata_df$study_id)
lcms_df <- lcms_df %>% dplyr::filter(rownames(.) %in% metadata_df$study_id)
spca_integrated_df <- spca_integrated_df %>% dplyr::filter(rownames(.) %in% metadata_df$study_id)
```


**Scaling** — when metadata columns are used as covariates, they need to be scaled so that each has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

```{r}
metadata_scaled_df <- metadata_df
metadata_scaled_df[,-c(1,3,5,6,8)] <- apply(metadata_df[,-c(1,3,5,6,8)],2,scale)
metadata_scaled_df <- metadata_scaled_df %>%
  mutate(sex=as.factor(sex),
         country=as.factor(country),
         group=as.factor(group),
         diet_supplements=as.factor(diet_supplements))
```

# SPCA

The sPCA dataset was created by concatenating the LC-MS and NMR datasets and applying the mixOmics::spca() function. See the preprocessing script for details. 

mixOmics::spca() performs **sparse Principal Component Analysis (sPCA)**, which works like regular PCA but adds a sparsity constraint so that only a subset of variables contributes to each component.
The degree of sparsity is controlled by a penalization term, which makes the components easier to interpret because irrelevant or noisy variables are given loadings of zero.

```{r,fig.width=4,fig.height=3}
              color_col = "hpdi_avg",
              perform_pca = FALSE)
```

## PERMANOVA

The test shows how much of the variation in the metabolome is explained by sex, age, BMI, vegan duration, country, and **hPDI**.

Variables were added sequentially (Type I sums of squares), so each p-value and R² reflects a partial effect after adjusting for the variables above it. The model first accounts for variation due to sex, age, vegan diet duration, BMI, and country of origin. It then accounts for the main effect of PDI, and finally tests whether the effect of PDI varies by country of origin (the interaction term).

----------------------

PDI explains **1.873%** of the variation after adjusting for sex, age, BMI, country, and diet duration. This result is statistically significant (p=0.001).

```{r}
# Create Euclidean distance matrix
dist_mat <- vegdist(spca_integrated_df, 
                    method = "euclidean")

# Test whether vegan vs omnivore differ in metabolomics
adonis_result <- adonis2(
  dist_mat ~ sex + bmi + age + vegan_duration + country*hpdi_avg,
  data = metadata_scaled_df , 
  permutations = 999,
  by="terms")

print(adonis_result)
```

```{r,fig.width=6,fig.height=2}
adonis_result <- adonis_result[-c(7,9),] %>% rownames_to_column("Var")
adonis_result$Var <- factor(adonis_result$Var,levels = rev(c("sex","bmi","age", "vegan_duration","country","hpdi_avg", "Residual")))
p <- ggplot(adonis_result, aes(fill=Var, x=R2, y="Metabolome")) + 
    geom_bar(position="stack", stat="identity") + 
  ylab("") + xlab("Partial variance explained (R²)") + 
  scale_fill_manual(values=rev(c("#ffffcc","#b3cde3","#ccebc5",
                                 "#decbe4","#fed9a6","darkred",
                                 "lightgrey")),name = "Covariate")  

p <- ggtheme(p)

p

p_pca[[2]] <- p
p_pca[[3]] <- adonis_result
```

## Univariate analysis

We test the differences between diets and hPDI using a generalized linear model, while adjusting for covariates.

### Continuous analysis

A GLM is used to identify which metabolites are significantly related to the hPDI score, adjusting for age, sex, country, and dietary group:

Metabolite ~ sex + bmi + age + eq_vegan_dur_total + Country*hPDI

# Metabolite-based hPDI

## Continuous univariate test

To build a vegan index from the concatenated dataset, we use linear regression to obtain coefficients for the significant variables identified across the analysis:

```{r}
final_significance
sign <- final_significance
```


```{r}
# define the variables
plot_list <- list()
rhos <- rep(NA,5)
ps <- rep(NA,5)

# split the datasets for cross-validation
concat_for_index <- concat_for_uni[sample(rownames(concat_for_uni)),]
set.seed(123)
cv_splits <- cv_folds(concat_for_index,folds = 5)

final_df_veganindex <- data.frame()

# cross validation loop
vars_selection <- list()
for (i in 1:length(cv_splits)){
  unisub_df <- concat_for_uni[cv_splits[[i]]$train,]
  results_list <- lapply(colnames(concat_integrated_df), 
                       function(x) fit_glm(x,unisub_df,
                                           tested_variable = "hpdi_avg"))
  results_df <- do.call(rbind, results_list)
  
  results_df$p_adjusted <- p.adjust(results_df$Pr...t..,method = "BH")

  vars <- results_df$metabolite[results_df$p_adjusted<0.05 & results_df$variable=="hpdi_avg"]
  vars_selection[[i]] <- vars
  
  # Wrap all variable names in backticks
  vars_safe <- paste0("`", vars, "`")
  
  fml <- as.formula(paste("hpdi_avg ~", paste(vars_safe, collapse = " + ")))
  
  # fit the model
  model <- lm(fml, unisub_df)
  
  # predict the result on validation dataset
  VG_index <- stats::predict(model,concat_for_uni[cv_splits[[i]]$val,])
  
  # store the predicted index
  sub_df <- concat_for_uni[cv_splits[[i]]$val,]
  sub_df$VGindex <- VG_index
  final_df_veganindex <- rbind(final_df_veganindex,sub_df)
  
  # calculate correlation 
  cor_test <- cor.test(sub_df$VGindex,
               sub_df$hpdi_avg,
               method = "spearman")
  cor_val <- cor_test$estimate
  if (cor_test$p.value >0.05) cor_val = 0

  # plot the result
  p <- ggplot(sub_df, 
              aes_string(x = "VGindex", y = "hpdi_avg"),
              color="blue") +
       geom_point() + 
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
    theme_minimal() + 
    ggtitle(paste("Rho =",round(cor_val,2)))

  plot_list[[i]] <- p
  rhos[i] <- round(cor_val,2)
  ps[i] <- cor_test$p.value
}

```

```{r}
mean(rhos)
```

```{r}
# Fisher's method to combine p-values
library(metap)
combined_p <- sumlog(ps)$p
combined_p
```

## Forest plot

```{r, fig.height=15,fig.width=5}
# Define custom colours
PDI_colors <- c("1st_hPDItertile"="#D73027",
               "2nd_hPDItertile"="orange",
               "3rd_hPDItertile"="#1A9850")

# Optional: order metabolites by mean effect size
forest_df <- pdi_effects %>%
  group_by(metabolite) %>%
  mutate(mean_eff = mean(emmean)) %>%
  ungroup()

forest_df$metabolite <- factor(
  forest_df$metabolite,
  levels = forest_df %>% 
    arrange(mean_eff) %>% 
    pull(metabolite) %>% 
    unique()
)

# Forest plot WITHOUT ANY TEXT LABELS
p_forest <- ggplot(forest_df, 
                   aes(x = emmean, 
                       y = metabolite, 
                       color = tertile_label)) +

  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower.CL, xmax = upper.CL), height = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +

  scale_color_manual(values = VS_colors) +

  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +

  labs(
    x = "Estimated mean (with 95% CI)",
    color = "hPDI"
  )

p_forest
```
